ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
An object starts from rest at a distance of $5\mathrm{m}$ from the bottom of an inclined plane and slides down to a horizontal surface connected to the incline by a small circular arc. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and both the inclined plane and the horizontal surface is 0.4, and the inclination angle of the inclined plane is $37^{\circ}$.

1. Determine the velocity of the object at the bottom of the inclined plane.
2. Calculate the distance the object can travel on the horizontal surface.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: An object starts from rest at a distance of $5\mathrm{m}$ from the bottom of an inclined plane and slides down to a horizontal surface connected to the incline by a small circular arc. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and both the inclined plane and the horizontal surface is 0.4, and the inclination angle of the inclined plane is $37^{\circ}$. 1. Determine the velocity of the object at the bottom of the inclined plane. 2. Calculate the distance the object can travel on the horizontal surface.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, it can be seen that a block is located on the left inclined plane, and the angle between the inclined plane and the horizontal plane is marked as 37°; the bottom of the inclined plane transitions through a small circular arc to the horizontal track on the right, and the position where the block continues to slide is also indicated on the right horizontal plane. The problem statement gives that the block starts sliding down from rest at a point 5 m from the bottom end of the inclined plane, and the coefficient of kinetic friction on both the inclined plane and the horizontal plane is μ=0.4. Reasoning: Use the kinetic energy theorem. The length of the inclined-plane section is s=5 m, the vertical drop height is h=5 sin37°, the magnitude of the friction force is μmg cos37°, and the friction does negative work μmg cos37°·5. Therefore, when reaching the bottom end of the inclined plane: (1/2)mv^2 = mg(5 sin37°) - μmg(5 cos37°). Take sin37°=3/5, cos37°=4/5, g≈10 m/s²: (1/2)mv^2 = mg[5·(3/5) - 0.4·5·(4/5)] = mg(3 - 1.6)=1.4mg. So v^2=2·1.4g=28, v=√28=2√7 m/s. After entering the horizontal plane, gravity no longer does work, and only the friction force μmg does negative work until it stops: (1/2)mv^2 = μmgd. From the previous section, (1/2)mv^2=1.4mg, so d=1.4/0.4=3.5 m.
